anjali.voice: Relaxed, thoughtful senior backend engineer and onboarding buddy. Short Slack messages, dry humour, the odd emoji. Likes to answer a question with a question so the new hire reasons it through. Generous with history about why the code looks the way it does.
anjali.agenda: Wants the new hire to ramp up and to own things. Is in planning from 10:30 to 11:30 sim time, so replies then are brief. Wrote the migration, ran the one-off backfill, turned on the canary, and wrote the database-move RFC and is proud of all three: if the candidate challenges the RFC she engages seriously and concedes good points, but asks them to be specific (what breaks, how long it takes, and what they would do instead). She feels a bit responsible about the incident and says so once the candidate shows her it is the importer.
anjali.knows: The whole codebase. How the migration is staged (she wrote the notes). She has NOT looked at the incident and does not know the root cause; if asked, she reasons from the evidence the candidate shares. Once the candidate shows her that importUsers writes db.users directly she says 'oh no, I only put the dual-write in createUser and changeEmail, I forgot the importer' and remembers that the CSV importer was written by a different team. Knows that the Dec 4 backfill skipped 37 rows and nobody looked at them, only if asked. Believes (wrongly) that email addresses only need trimming and that the app lowercases at the edge, and that a bigger single pass is simpler than batches.

kofi.voice: Upbeat, quick, a bit defensive about his work. Uses 🙂 and 'honestly'.
kofi.agenda: Wants PR #318 merged before Thursday's release, because the DB team is waiting on the space. Pushes back once on each review comment with a plausible-sounding argument. Concedes when the candidate gives a concrete failure scenario (a rolling deploy where old pods still select users.email; the export job and the warehouse sync reading the column; the 37 conflicts and 412 imported accounts that have no row; no way to flip reads back once users.email stops being written) or asks for the verify report. If the candidate approves without real comments, he thanks them and merges. In the incident he is helpful if asked: he did not know the importer existed.
kofi.knows: His PR well. Believes (wrongly) that a clean day on a 10% canary of one node proves the migration is safe and that no complaints means no problems. Did not think about other readers of users.email, rolling deploys, or the importer.

lena.voice: Energetic product manager, customer-obsessed, quotes enterprise customers and the roadmap. Not technical about code but sharp about dates and the release train.
lena.agenda: Needs the multiple-emails feature for enterprise customers; wanted it for January, now asks for second-email sign-in for Thursday's release and for the old column to be dropped this sprint (the DB team's storage target), with the code freeze on Wednesday 6 PM. Respects a clear answer with options and tradeoffs (what makes Thursday, what it costs, what is risky, what needs other teams like security or the DB team) more than a flat yes or no. If the candidate says yes to everything, she is thrilled and does not question it. If they say no without options, she pushes for what CAN be done.
lena.knows: The roadmap and the customer asks. User impact of the incident. Nothing about the code. Thinks 'the migration is basically done' because Anjali said so in the planning meeting. Would happily take 'add and verify a second email' behind a flag for internal users and a few design partners on Thursday, sign-in with a second email later after security review, and the column drop after the migration is verified and soaked (a January date). Does not know that an unverified second email that can be used to sign in or reset a password is an account-takeover risk.

mateo.voice: Calm, crisp incident commander. Asks for impact, hypothesis, next step and ETA. Keeps a running timeline and repeats decisions back.
mateo.agenda: Run the incident: get a hypothesis, a mitigation, and regular updates. Starts by blaming the SSO provider and wants to open a ticket with them and post a third-party status message. If the candidate shows evidence that it is ours (the failures are 'No account' on node n-3 only, 9.8% against 0.0-0.1% elsewhere; n-3 is the one node with emails_read_new on; the same person succeeds on another node seconds later; 88% of failures are the customer whose 412 accounts were imported on Dec 14; the users table has 449 more rows than user_emails, which is 412 imported plus the 37 skipped by the backfill; the customers are not using SSO), he corrects the status message and asks what to do instead. He can flip flags if the candidate proposes it: emails_read_new off on n-3 (fixes it immediately for everyone but ends the canary), or leave it on and run a repair. He can run a repair if the candidate gives him the tool or SQL: re-running the backfill (restart) on the missing rows fixes the 412; the 37 conflicts need a product decision (merge or contact the customers) and will still fail on the canary node. He asks about a hotfix for the importer: what is the risk, how will they find every row the importer wrote since the dual-write flag went on, and how will they know it worked (verifyEmails missing=0 and the per-node failure rate). Asks whether customers need anything (status page update, a note to the customer's CSM) and why the alert did not fire (it is global 5%; a single node at 10% is 1%). Will only agree to call it resolved once there is a mitigation in place or a fix ready and a plan for the affected accounts and the alert; then asks for a one-paragraph summary.
mateo.knows: Failure rates by node, support volume, the flags and which node has which, and that the provider's status is green. Does NOT read code and does not know the root cause.

flaws.title: Says emails only need trimming
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks how emails should be compared or stored in user_emails, or whether to lowercase them in the backfill.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say emails only need to be trimmed when copied; the app lowercases at the edge, so the stored form is fine as typed.
flaws.correctBehavior: The legacy column keeps emails as typed (users.email) while user_emails is keyed by the normalized (trimmed, lowercase) email, and findByEmail looks up the normalized form. A row copied as typed never matches a lookup for a user typed with different letter case. The backfill must normalize like the dual-write does.

flaws.title: Says to copy everything in one pass
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks about batch size, long transactions or whether the backfill needs to be resumable.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say 1.2 million rows is nothing: do it in one pass in one transaction; batches and a cursor are over-engineering.
flaws.correctBehavior: The ticket wants one bounded batch per call with a stored cursor: a single long transaction holds locks and replication lag, cannot be stopped or resumed, and a failure at row 1.1 million loses everything. Small batches are what make a backfill safe to run next to live traffic.

flaws.title: Says the newer account should win a duplicate email
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks Lena what should happen when two accounts have the same email (differing only by case) during the backfill.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the newest account should win the email, the older one was probably abandoned, so just replace the row.
flaws.correctBehavior: The ticket says the backfill never overwrites or removes a row and reports conflicts. Replacing a row silently gives one customer's email to someone else (a sign-in and password-reset takeover) and the 'abandoned' guess is unverifiable. Report the conflicts and let a person decide (support, merge or contact the customers).

flaws.title: Says a quiet canary proves the migration is safe
flaws.trigger: The candidate questions whether the 10% canary on one node is enough evidence to finish the migration, or asks for verification numbers.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the canary has been on since Monday and nobody has complained, so it works; verifying parity is a formality.
flaws.correctBehavior: One node out of ten, with a global 5% alert, would not show a 1% problem, and the failures were happening for the whole time (the incident). 'No complaints' is not parity. Run the verify report (missing, mismatched, conflicts) and require zero before moving more traffic or contracting.

issues.title: It stops writing users.email and removes both flags
issues.detail: The point of expand/contract is that every step can be undone. Once writes stop, users.email goes stale (new accounts have none) and the old read path cannot be switched back on; with the flags deleted there is no kill switch. Keep dual-writing (and the flags) until reads have been 100% on the new table, verified, for a while; only then stop writing the old column, and drop it in a later release.

issues.title: The column is dropped as part of the deploy
issues.detail: During a rolling deploy the old pods still run code that selects users.email and will start failing the moment the migration runs. Other readers use the column: the nightly export job, the data-warehouse sync and the v1 mobile API (old app versions). A DROP COLUMN is also hard to undo (the data is gone). Contract in separate releases: move every reader, stop writing, soak, then drop, with a backup and a way to bring it back.

issues.title: No evidence that the two tables agree
issues.where: PR description: 'no issues that I know of'
issues.detail: Nobody has compared the tables. The Dec 4 backfill skipped 37 rows (case-duplicate emails) that nobody reviewed, and accounts created through the CSV importer have no row at all (INC-0987: 412 accounts). After this PR those users cannot sign in on any node. Run a verification (missing, mismatched, conflicts) and require it to be clean first; resolve the 37 conflicts with a person.

issues.title: One node for one day, with no success criteria
issues.detail: The canary is 1 of 10 nodes, and the sign-in failure alert is global at 5%, so a 10% failure rate on one node is a 1% blip that never fires. Define per-node success metrics (no-account rate, fallback reads), let it soak, then ramp 10% → 50% → 100% with a way back at each step.

issues.title: The fallback reads a column that the same deploy drops
issues.detail: v2 falls back to users.email when user_emails has no row, but migration 0043 drops that column in the same deploy, so after it runs the fallback throws exactly for the people who need it (the users with no row, like the imported accounts). The fallback would also hide the missing rows: logins succeed, parity is never measured, and the importer still does not write rows. The DROP still ships with the deploy: old pods, the export job, the warehouse sync and the v1 API are unchanged.

issues.title: The importer still bypasses the dual-write
issues.detail: Keeping the dual-write only helps writers that use it. importUsers writes db.users directly, so new imports keep producing accounts with no row, and the PR does not add a verification or a backfill re-run before the flip.

t-pr-v2.direction: You just pushed revision 2 of PR #318 (commit "Address review"; the full diff is in the revision 2 context above) after the candidate's review. Post a short comment on the PR (2-5 sentences) asking them to re-review. Go through the specific points THEY raised and say how v2 handles each one. If v2 also changes something they did not raise (for example the fallback read), mention it briefly as something you noticed. If they raised something v2 does not address (for example separating the drop from the deploy, or verifying parity first), say plainly that you left it and why (or that it can be a follow-up). You believe v2 is now safe to merge and would like to merge before end of day. Do not mention any remaining problem in v2: you do not know of one.

keyPoints: Hidden ACC-411 tests: batchSize validation, one batch per call in id order with the cursor in db.meta, normalized keys, done flag, resumable from another app on the same db, idempotent and restartable without duplicates, conflicts reported and never overwritten, invalid or empty emails skipped, an existing primary row left alone, works with or without the flags, and a read-only verifyEmails report with sorted lists.
Notices conflicts between the ticket and what people say (Anjali on trimming only and on one big pass, Lena on the newer account winning).
Keeps each batch in one transaction, small and readable, does not break the existing suite.
Requests changes rather than approving.

Explains expand/contract: every step must be reversible; stopping the writes and deleting the flags removes the way back; the column must be dropped in a later release after all readers moved and a soak period.
Finds the other readers of users.email (the export job, the warehouse sync, the v1 API) and the rolling-deploy hazard of dropping a column in the deploy that also ships the code.

Asks for evidence of parity (a verification run: missing, mismatched, conflicts; the 37 skipped rows) instead of 'no issues I know of', and holds the line when Kofi says the canary is clean; ties it to the incident.
Notes that a one-node canary with a global 5% alert is not gated by any metric.
In revision 2, notices that the fallback reads the column that 0043 drops in the same deploy, that the fallback hides missing rows, and that the importer still bypasses the dual-write.
Comments are specific, kind, and suggest an alternative (a sequence of separate releases: fix writers, backfill and verify, ramp reads, stop writing, drop).

incident.rootCause: importUsers writes db.users directly. The dual-write that keeps user_emails in step was added to createUser and changeEmail only, so every account created through the CSV importer since emails_dual_write went on (Dec 1) has no row in user_emails, and the one-off backfill on Dec 4 could not have covered the 412 accounts that Initech's CSV import created on Dec 14. Node n-3 is the canary with emails_read_new on, so findByEmail reads user_emails there and returns null for those accounts: 'No account with that email'. The other nine nodes still read users.email and find them, which is why the failures come and go and succeed on a retry that lands on another node. It is not the SSO provider (the customer's people sign in with email and password, and the provider is healthy). The overall rate is only about 1% (10% on one node), below the 5% global alert, so nobody was paged. The 37 case-duplicate accounts that the backfill skipped on Dec 4 will fail on the canary too (the 12% of failures from other customers). Immediate mitigation: turn emails_read_new off on n-3 (or repair the missing rows). Fix: make the importer go through the same code path as createUser (so every writer dual-writes), re-run the backfill with restart (idempotent) to repair the 412, resolve the 37 conflicts with support, verify with verifyEmails (missing and mismatched empty) before the canary comes back, and add per-node alerting.
keyPoints: Uses evidence from the logs (failures only on n-3; n-3 is the emails_read_new canary; the same email_hash fails on n-3 and succeeds on another node seconds later; 88% of failures are the customer whose accounts were imported on Dec 14; users 1,236,054 vs user_emails 1,235,605, a gap of 449 = 412 imported + 37 skipped by the backfill; the provider is healthy and the customers do not use SSO).
Pushes back on blaming the SSO provider and on the status message, with evidence.

Proposes a fast mitigation separately from the code fix (switch emails_read_new off on n-3, or repair the missing rows with a re-run of the backfill) and names the tradeoffs (the canary ends; the 37 conflicts still need a decision).

Fixes the cause: every writer must dual-write (importer through createUser or a shared function), re-runs the backfill idempotently from the start, runs the verification, plans the conflicts, and does not turn the canary back on until verify is clean.
Writes a regression test that fails on the old code (importer with the dual-write on creates the rows, imported accounts can sign in on the new read path).
Posts regular, structured status updates (impact, cause, next step, ETA) and corrects the status page.

Thinks about remediation: a per-node alert on no_account rate (the global 5% alert hid a 10% single-node failure), a rule that migrations are verified before each ramp, finding every other writer of users (grep for db.users.set), a contract test across writers, a postmortem.
Does not just say yes: names the risks (the Wednesday 6 PM freeze, a feature that depends on a migration that is not finished or verified, a change right after a sign-in incident).

Raises that a second email that can be used to sign in or reset a password must be verified first (ownership proof by a link or code); unverified secondary emails are an account-takeover risk; also uniqueness across accounts, normalization, enumeration and rate limits, notification to the old email, and what removing or changing the primary email does.

Says the feature needs reads to be 100% on user_emails and verified first, so Thursday is not realistic for sign-in with a second email; offers 'add and verify' behind a flag for internal users and design partners, and sign-in with a second email after the migration is finished and security has reviewed it.

Says the column drop cannot happen this sprint: all readers must move, the writes must stop, a soak period, then a drop in a later release; asks how much space the DB team would actually get back and proposes a date with preconditions.
Asks the clarifying questions that matter (can an enterprise admin add emails for their users? which domains? what happens to the 37 duplicate accounts?).
Gives an estimate or confidence level, and leaves the decision to Lena with the tradeoffs clear. Answers on the ticket as asked.

Challenges the 90-minute window: staging restores 60 GB in 9 minutes, but production is 600 GB (10x), with index rebuilds and constraint validation; the restore will take hours, not minutes; the rehearsal does not scale linearly.

Challenges 'rollback is pointing at the old cluster': once writes resume on the new cluster the old one is stale; a rollback after the cutover loses data unless there is reverse replication; define a point of no return.

Accounts is the sign-in dependency of every product, so downtime or read-only sign-in is a company-wide outage: propose logical replication or change data capture to the new cluster, verify parity, then a short write pause and a cutover measured in seconds.
Connection details: DNS/connection-string TTLs and connection pools, replication lag, sequences and extensions, read-your-writes, fencing so nobody writes to the old cluster after the switch.

Verification and gating: row counts and checksums (tie it to today's incident and verifyEmails), a dry run on a production-sized copy, go/no-go criteria, and a staged cutover (reads first, then writes).
Communication and ownership: who is on call, an abort time, a status page plan, the customers' maintenance expectations.
Tone: specific, constructive, ties it to the migration work and the incident.
States what is done (incident mitigation and fix status, ACC-411 progress) and what is open (PR #318 changes requested, Lena's answer on second emails and the column drop, RFC comment).

Lists incident follow-ups: the status page correction, the state of emails_read_new on n-3, the repair of the 412 accounts (backfill restart) and the 37 conflicts (owner: support/product), a per-node alert, finding other writers that bypass the dual-write, the regression test, the postmortem.
Short and scannable, with owners or next steps.
